# Upakkilesa Sutta (MN 128 (PTS MN iii 152))

**Title (Pali):** Upakkilesa Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** Corruptions

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Upakkilesa Sutta* (MN 128) is structured into two main parts [Rogell 2003]. In the first part, set against the backdrop of the dispute among the mendicants at Kosambī, the Buddha fails to reconcile the quarreling community and departs for the wilderness, delivering a series of stanzas on concord and non-hatred [Rogell 2003]. He subsequently visits Anuruddha and his companions, who are dwelling in harmony [Analayo 2017b]. There, Anuruddha reports that although they experienced meditative light and the vision of forms (*obhāsa* and *rūpa*), the experience ceased because they failed to penetrate the sign (*nimitta*) [Analayo 2017b; Polak 2011]. In response, the Buddha recounts his own pre-awakening meditative struggles, enumerating mental obstructions (*upakkilesa*)—such as doubt, inattention, sloth-and-torpor, apprehension, and elation—that cause concentration to deteriorate and inner light to vanish [Analayo 2016; Stanley et al. 2018; Analayo 2017b]. After eliminating these corruptions, the Buddha cultivated a threefold scheme of concentration: with initial and sustained application (*savitakka savicāra*), without initial application but with sustained application (*avitakka vicāramatta*), and without either (*avitakka avicāra*) [Analayo 2016; Bodhi 2007; Polak 2011]. This intermediate category serves as a key scriptural precursor for the fivefold *jhāna* classification in the Abhidhamma tradition [Bodhi 2007].

Scholars have noted that the text presents the perception of light and forms not as the object of concentration itself, but rather as a natural byproduct reflecting the clarity and stability of the mind [Hung 2010; Analayo 2019; Polak 2011]. Although the Pāli commentary (*Papañcasūdanī*) assigns this meditative struggle to the night of the Buddha's awakening, modern comparative analysis demonstrates that the gradual cultivation of these states across days and nights occurred much earlier, likely prior to his training under Āḷāra Kālāma and Uddaka Rāmaputta [Analayo 2016; Stanley et al. 2018; Analayo 2017b].

Curated parallels include the *Madhyama-āgama* version (*MĀ* 72 / *Changshouwang benqi jing*), *EĀ* 24.8, Sanskrit manuscript fragments (SHT sutta75, SF 13), and parallel episodes across various Vinaya recensions, including the Pāli *Kosambakakkhandhaka* (Kd 10), the *Kośāmbakavastu* of the *Mūlasarvāstivādivinaya*, and Chinese Vinayas [Hung 2010]. The opening narrative and verse portions share text with the *Dhammapada*, *Patna Dharmapada*, *Udānavarga*, and the *Cūḷagosiṅga Sutta* (MN 31). DharmaNexus matches strongly support these alignments, recording extensive Pali-internal text reuse with Kd 10 (§5.1–14.9) and MN 31 (§8.2–15.2), as well as cross-language correspondences with the *Madhyama-āgama* (T 26), the Sanskrit *Kośāmbakavastu*, and Tibetan Vinaya collections [DharmaNexus].
